claim: Protein aggregation appears to originate from partially unfolded conformations that are sampled through stochastic fluctuations of the native protein.
source: Protein aggregation appears to originate from partially unfolded conformations that are sampled through stochastic fluctuations of the native protein.
evidence: This is a general statement about protein aggregation mechanisms, supported by established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The conformational dynamics of the full-length (23-231) mouse prion protein were studied under native conditions using photoinduced electron transfer coupled to fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (PET-FCS).
source: Here, the conformational dynamics of the full-length (23-231) mouse prion protein were studied under native conditions, using photoinduced electron transfer coupled to fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (PET-FCS).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, as stated in the abstract.

claim: The slowest fluctuations observed by PET-FCS could be associated with the folding of the unfolded state to an intermediate state.
source: The slowest fluctuations could be associated with the folding of the unfolded state to an intermediate state, by the use of microsecond mixing experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by microsecond mixing experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The two faster fluctuations observed by PET-FCS could be attributed to fluctuations within the native state ensemble.
source: The two faster fluctuations observed by PET-FCS, could be attributed to fluctuations within the native state ensemble.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the PET-FCS data and supporting analyses.

claim: The addition of salt, which is known to initiate the aggregation of the protein, resulted in an enhancement in the time scale of fluctuations in the core of the protein.
source: The addition of salt, which is known to initiate the aggregation of the protein, resulted in an enhancement in the time scale of fluctuations in the core of the protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by PET-FCS experiments conducted with and without salt.

claim: Native state dynamics are important in initiating the aggregation of proteins.
source: The results indicate the importance of native state dynamics in initiating the aggregation of proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: Structural fluctuations in proteins are critical for function.
source: Structural fluctuations in proteins are not only critical for function (Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007; Yang et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Structural fluctuations in proteins are critical for folding.
source: Structural fluctuations in proteins are not only critical for function (Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007; Yang et al., 2014) and folding (Wani and Udgaonkar, 2009; Malhotra and Udgaonkar, 2016; Frauenfelder et al., 1991; Bai et al., 1995)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Structural fluctuations in proteins have a role to play in protein misfolding and aggregation.
source: Structural fluctuations in proteins are not only critical for function (Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007; Yang et al., 2014) and folding (Wani and Udgaonkar, 2009; Malhotra and Udgaonkar, 2016; Frauenfelder et al., 1991; Bai et al., 1995), but also have a role to play in protein misfolding and aggregation (Scheibel, 2001; Elam et al., 2003; Chiti and Dobson, 2009; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Thermal fluctuations can lead to the sampling of partially unfolded conformations.
source: Thermal fluctuations can lead to the sampling of partially unfolded conformations, which may or may not be populated transiently on protein folding and unfolding pathways (Matouschek and Fersht, 1993; Sridevi and Udgaonkar, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Partially unfolded conformations sampled through thermal fluctuations may be aggregation-prone.
source: Thermal fluctuations can lead to the sampling of partially unfolded conformations, which may or may not be populated transiently on protein folding and unfolding pathways (Matouschek and Fersht, 1993; Sridevi and Udgaonkar, 2002), and which may be aggregation-prone (Hamid Wani and Udgaonkar, 2006; Moulick and Udgaonkar, 2017; Booth et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 85% of prion diseases occur in a sporadic manner, presumably through stochastic fluctuations in the native state of the protein.
source: This is particularly true in the case of the prion protein, because 85% of prion diseases occur in a sporadic manner, presumably through stochastic fluctuations in the native state of the protein.
evidence: This claim combines a statistical fact about prion diseases with a speculative mechanism.

claim: The prion protein has a structure that is highly dynamic, as reflected in its unusually high native state heat capacity.
source: In this context, it is important to note that the prion protein has a structure that is highly dynamic, as reflected in its unusually high native state heat capacity (Moulick and Udgaonkar, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Misfolding and aggregation of the prion protein are linked to several fatal neurodegenerative diseases.
source: In the case of the prion protein, misfolding and aggregation are linked to several fatal neurodegenerative diseases (Collinge, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The cellular form of the prion protein, PrPC, is composed of an unstructured N-terminal region and a structured C-terminal domain that is comprised of three α-helices (α1, α2, α3) and two short β-strands (β1, β2).
source: The cellular form of the prion protein, PrPC, is composed of an unstructured N-terminal region, and a structured C-terminal domain that is comprised of three α-helices (α1, α2, α3) and two short β-strands (β1, β2) (Riek et al., 1996).
evidence: This structural description is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Prion disease is caused by the infectious scrapie form, PrPSc, which is multimeric, β-sheet rich, partially resistant to proteinase K digestion.
source: Prion disease is caused by the infectious scrapie form, PrPSc, which is multimeric, β-sheet rich, partially resistant to proteinase K digestion (Caughey et al., 1991)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PrPSc is capable of forming amyloid fibrils.
source: Prion disease is caused by the infectious scrapie form, PrPSc, which is multimeric, β-sheet rich, partially resistant to proteinase K digestion (Caughey et al., 1991), and is capable of forming amyloid fibrils (Prusiner, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spontaneous conversion of PrPC to PrPSc appears to occur in 85% of prion diseases.
source: Spontaneous conversion of PrPC to PrPSc, appears to occur in 85% of prion diseases, but the nature and time scales of prion protein dynamics that dictate this conformational conversion are not well understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of spontaneous conversion in prion diseases.

claim: Sub-domain separation of β-strands β1 and β2, along with helix1 (α1) from the core helices α2 and α3, initiates the aggregation of the prion protein.
source: It has been suggested that sub-domain separation of β-strands, β1 and β2, along with helix1 (α1) from the core helices, α2 and α3, initiates the aggregation of the prion protein (Eghiaian et al., 2007) (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The aggregation of pathogenic and stabilized variants of mouse prion protein (moPrP) has been shown to proceed through a similar sub-domain separation mechanism.
source: The aggregation of pathogenic (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a) and stabilized (Singh et al., 2014) variants of mouse prion protein (moPrP) has also been shown to proceed through a similar sub-domain separation mechanism (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Native state HDX studies carried out under conditions that facilitate prion misfolding and aggregation identified partially unfolded forms (PUFs) in equilibrium with the N state, which have been implicated in the aggregation of the protein.
source: Native state HDX studies carried out under conditions that facilitate prion misfolding and aggregation, identified partially unfolded forms (PUFs) in equilibrium with the N state, which have been implicated in the aggregation of the protein (Moulick et al., 2015; Moulick and Udgaonkar, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The prion protein folds and unfolds within a millisecond.
source: Moreover, because the prion protein folds and unfolds within a millisecond (Honda et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Studies of the folding and unfolding of several prion proteins have identified states intermediate in their structures to the structures of the native (N) and unfolded (U) states, whose accumulation has been linked to prion protein aggregation.
source: Studies of the folding and unfolding of several prion proteins have identified states intermediate in their structures to the structures of the native (N) and unfolded (U) states, whose accumulation has been linked to prion protein aggregation (Apetri and Surewicz, 2002; Apetri et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2011; Honda et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native state.
source: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native (Doose et al., 2009; Ries et al., 2014; Neuweiler et al., 2009), unfolded (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Daidone et al., 2010) and intermediate states (Neuweiler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the unfolded state.
source: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native (Doose et al., 2009; Ries et al., 2014; Neuweiler et al., 2009), unfolded (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Daidone et al., 2010) and intermediate states (Neuweiler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in intermediate states.
source: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native (Doose et al., 2009; Ries et al., 2014; Neuweiler et al., 2009), unfolded (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Daidone et al., 2010) and intermediate states (Neuweiler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Conformational dynamics across helices α1 and α3, and across helices α2 and α3, were monitored separately in two mutant variants of the protein designed for PET-FCS measurements.
source: Conformational dynamics across helices α1 and α3, and across helices α2 and α3, were monitored separately in two mutant variants of the protein designed for PET-FCS measurements (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Quenching of an Atto 655 moiety by a suitably placed Trp residue occurs when the two come within contact quenching distance (<1 nm).
source: In each mutant variant, the dynamics leading to the quenching of an Atto 655 moiety introduced into the protein, by a suitably placed Trp residue, when the two come within contact quenching distance (<1 nm) (Vaiana et al., 2003), was measured as fluctuations in the Atto 655 fluorescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Autocorrelation functions (ACFs) for both the distances show three exponential processes, arising from sub-millisecond dynamics in the protein.
source: Autocorrelation functions (ACFs) for both the distances show three exponential processes, arising from sub-millisecond dynamics in the protein.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the PET-FCS experiments.

claim: The slow exponential process was found to represent the dynamics of folding from the U state to an intermediate state (I), by comparing the kinetics obtained from PET-FCS to the kinetics of folding of the Atto 655-labeled protein.
source: The slow exponential process was found to represent the dynamics of folding from the U state to an intermediate state (I), by comparing the kinetics obtained from PET-FCS to the kinetics of folding of the Atto 655-labeled protein.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PET-FCS data with microsecond mixing experiments.

claim: The two faster exponential processes could be attributed to fluctuations in the native state.
source: The two faster exponential processes could be attributed to fluctuations in the native state.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: The native state dynamics of moPrP result in global unfolding via an intermediate.
source: Overall, it is shown that the native state dynamics of moPrP result in global unfolding via an intermediate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Labeling with Atto 655 did not result in any alteration in the secondary structure of the protein, as indicated by the far-UV circular dichroism measurements.
source: Labeling with Atto 655 did not result in any alteration in the secondary structure of the protein, as indicated by the far-UV circular dichroism measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PET quenching occurs primarily by a static quenching mechanism.
source: It is known that such quenching occurs primarily by a static quenching mechanism (Sauer and Neuweiler, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PET from the Trp side-chain occurs within a few picoseconds.
source: Since PET occurs within a few picoseconds (Lakowicz, 1999; Zhong and Zewail, 2001; Doose et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The observed rate constant of the overall quenching reaction reflects the rate constant for the formation of the dye-Trp complex.
source: Since PET occurs within a few picoseconds (Lakowicz, 1999; Zhong and Zewail, 2001; Doose et al., 2005), and because dissociation of the dye-Trp complex is much slower (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Soranno et al., 2017), the observed rate constant of the overall quenching reaction reflects the rate constant for the formation of the dye-Trp complex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetics of PET and complex dissociation, supported by citations.

claim: The quenching distance, above which electron transfer cannot occur, is about 0.5 nm.
source: However, in PET, the probability of electron transfer decreases asymptotically to near zero within less than a nanometer of separation; and the quenching distance, above which electron transfer cannot occur, is about 0.5 nm (Lewis et al., 1997; Vaiana et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The ACFs of both W144/C199-Atto moPrP and W171/C225-Atto moPrP showed three exponential components, in addition to the diffusion component.
source: The ACFs of both W144/C199-Atto moPrP and W171/C225-Atto moPrP, showed three exponential components, in addition to the diffusion component (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the PET-FCS experiments, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The total amplitude of the exponential components for W144-C199-Atto moPrP was higher than that observed for W171/C225-Atto moPrP.
source: The total amplitude of the exponential components for W144-C199-Atto moPrP was higher than that observed for W171/C225-Atto moPrP.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results from the two constructs.

claim: The time constants and amplitudes of the exponential processes were found to be independent of the excitation power used in the FCS experiments.
source: The time constants and amplitudes of the exponential processes were found to be independent of the excitation power used in the FCS experiments (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a control experiment result, documented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The Trp-less control proteins showed negligible exponential components, confirming that these components originate from the quenching of the fluorescence of the Atto moiety attached to the protein by the Trp residue in the Trp-containing proteins.
source: The Trp-less control proteins showed negligible exponential components, confirming that these components originate from the quenching of the fluorescence of the Atto moiety attached to the protein by the Trp residue in the Trp-containing proteins (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 2.

claim: The hydrodynamic radius calculated from the diffusion coefficient obtained from the PET-FCS measurements was 2.8 nm, which matches well with the RH measured by dynamic light scattering experiments in earlier studies.
source: The hydrodynamic radius calculated from the diffusion coefficient obtained from the PET-FCS measurements was 2.8 nm, which matches well with the RH measured by dynamic light scattering experiments in earlier studies (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008).
evidence: This claim compares current measurements with previous DLS data, supported by a citation.

claim: The relative fluorescence intensity of the Trp-containing protein compared to Trp-less PET construct directly gives the fraction of molecules in the native state ensemble, in which the Atto 655 fluorescence is not quenched by PET from a Trp side-chain.
source: With the assumption that the quenched states are completely non-fluorescent, the relative fluorescence intensity of the Trp-containing protein compared to Trp-less PET construct directly gives the fraction of molecules in the native state ensemble, in which the Atto 655 fluorescence is not quenched by PET from a Trp side-chain.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on an assumption about the quenched states.

claim: Conformational fluctuations on the 0.5–20 µs time scale have been observed in the native state ensembles of other proteins.
source: Conformational fluctuations on this time scale have been observed in the native state ensembles of other proteins (Jensen et al., 2011; Ries et al., 2014; Schulze et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The unfolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in a single kinetic phase that accounted for the entire equilibrium unfolding amplitude of unfolding.
source: The unfolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in a single kinetic phase (Figure 3a) that accounted for the entire equilibrium unfolding amplitude of unfolding (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microsecond mixing experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Extrapolation of the denaturant dependence of the unfolding rate constant to zero urea concentration predicted an apparent unfolding rate constant of about 400 s−1 in native conditions.
source: Extrapolation of the denaturant dependence of the unfolding rate constant to zero urea concentration, predicted an apparent unfolding rate constant of about 400 s−1 in native conditions.
evidence: This is an extrapolation from experimental data.

claim: The refolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in two kinetic phases whose total amplitude accounted for the entire equilibrium amplitude of folding.
source: The refolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in two kinetic phases (Figure 3b), whose total amplitude accounted for the entire equilibrium amplitude of folding (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a direct observation from microsecond mixing experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The simplest explanation for the observation of two kinetic phases is that folding occurs via an U↔ I ↔ N mechanism, in which I is a folding intermediate.
source: The simplest explanation for the observation of two kinetic phases is that folding occurs via an U↔ I ↔ N mechanism, in which I is a folding intermediate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic data.

claim: The slow kinetic phase had a rate constant of ~500 s−1 and accounted for about 33% of the total amplitude of the decrease in fluorescence seen for folding from U to N.
source: The slow kinetic phase had a rate constant of ~500 s−1 (Figure 3d), and accounted for about 33% of the total amplitude of the decrease in fluorescence seen for folding from U to N.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the kinetic experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the fast phase observed in the microsecond mixing experiments extrapolates into the dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the slower exponential process observed in the PET-FCS measurements.
source: Figure 3d shows that the dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the fast phase observed in the microsecond mixing experiments, extrapolates into the dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the slower exponential process observed in the PET-FCS measurements.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing data in Figure 3d.

claim: The rate constant of the slow exponential process measured in 0.75 M urea by PET-FCS matches the fast rate constant of folding in 0.75 M urea.
source: It is also seen that the rate constant of the slow exponential process measured in 0.75 M urea by PET-FCS, matches the fast rate constant of folding in 0.75 M urea.
evidence: This is a comparison of rate constants from different experimental methods.

claim: The observation that the rate constant of the fast phase of folding observed in the microsecond mixing experiments was identical with the rate constant of the slow exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments indicated that the same transition was being monitored in both measurements.
source: The observation that the rate constant of the fast phase of folding observed in the microsecond mixing experiments was identical with the rate constant of the slow exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments, indicated that the same transition was being monitored in both measurements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of rate constants from two different methods.

claim: The slowest exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments represents a conformational fluctuation of the unfolded state at low concentrations of urea, which is not a random fluctuation, but which leads to the formation of a productive folding intermediate.
source: It is important to note that the slowest exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments, represents a conformational fluctuation of the unfolded state at low concentrations of urea, which is not a random fluctuation, but which leads to the formation of a productive folding intermediate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PET-FCS data in the context of folding.

claim: Salt is known to trigger the aggregation of moPrP at pH 4.
source: Salt is known to trigger the aggregation of moPrP at pH 4 (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2010; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016; Sengupta and Udgaonkar, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the presence of salt, the combined amplitude (K1 +K2) of the two faster exponential processes was found to have slightly increased for W171/C225-Atto moPrP.
source: In the presence of salt, the combined amplitude (K1 +K2) of the two faster exponential processes was found to have slightly increased for W171/C225-Atto moPrP (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from PET-FCS experiments with salt, shown in Figure 5.

claim: The time scale of the native state fluctuations was observed to become faster upon the addition of salt.
source: The time scale of the native state fluctuations was observed to become faster upon the addition of salt (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from PET-FCS experiments with salt, documented in Table 1.

claim: Equilibrium unfolding experiments carried out at pH four for W144/C199-Atto moPrP in the presence of salt indicated that the protein is destabilized by approximately 0.7 kcal/mol upon addition of salt.
source: Equilibrium unfolding experiments carried out at pH four for W144/C199-Atto moPrP in the presence of salt indicated that the protein is destabilized by approximately 0.7 kcal/mol upon addition of salt (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from equilibrium unfolding experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the amplitude and the time constant of the slowest exponential process was seen to decrease upon the addition of salt, at pH 4, for both the PET pairs.
source: Both the amplitude and the time constant of the slowest exponential process was seen to decrease upon the addition of salt, at pH 4, for both the PET pairs (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct observation from PET-FCS experiments with salt, documented in Table 1.

claim: The rate constant of the N → N** transition measured for the α2-α3 segment by monitoring fluctuations in W171/C225-Atto moPrP was nearly an order of magnitude slower than that measured for the α1-α3 segment, by monitoring fluctuations in W144/C199-Atto moPrP.
source: It was observed that the rate constant of the N → N** transition measured for the α2-α3 segment by monitoring fluctuations in W171/C225-Atto moPrP, was nearly an order of magnitude slower than that measured for the α1-α3 segment, by monitoring fluctuations in W144/C199-Atto moPrP (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a comparison of rate constants from the two constructs, shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The addition of salt had a significant effect on the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions measured for the α2-α3 segment, but had a negligible effect on the rate constants measured for the α1-α3 segment.
source: The addition of salt had a significant effect on the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions measured for the α2-α3 segment, but had a negligible effect on the rate constants measured for the α1-α3 segment (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a comparison of the effects of salt on the two constructs, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: A recent real-time NMR monitored aggregation study of moPrP has shown that the addition of salt causes the disruption of the salt bridge between residues K193 and E195, which triggers the aggregation process.
source: A recent real-time NMR monitored aggregation study of moPrP, has shown that the addition of salt causes the disruption of the salt bridge between residues K193 and E195, which triggers the aggregation process (Sengupta and Udgaonkar, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Earlier studies have indicated that the dynamics in the U state of prion protein play a role in initiating misfolding and oligomerisation.
source: Earlier studies have indicated that the dynamics in the U state of prion protein play a role in initiating misfolding and oligomerisation (Yu et al., 2012; Srivastava and Lapidus, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the current study it was shown that the fluctuations within the N state of the protein are responsible for the misfolding of the moPrP.
source: In the current study it was shown that the fluctuations within the N state of the protein are responsible for the misfolding of the moPrP.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of the current study.

claim: For several proteins, aggregation has been shown to proceed from partially folded intermediates on protein folding/unfolding pathways.
source: In the case of several proteins, aggregation has been shown to proceed from partially folded intermediates on protein folding/unfolding pathways (Fink, 1998; Hamid Wani and Udgaonkar, 2006; Jahn and Parker, 2006; De Simone et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A partially unfolded intermediate formed during the unfolding of the CTD of moPrP was shown directly to be the precursor conformation from which misfolding proceeds.
source: More recently, a partially unfolded intermediate formed during the unfolding of the CTD of moPrP, was shown directly to be the precursor conformation from which misfolding proceeds (Moulick and Udgaonkar, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Upon the addition of salt, N is destabilized by 0.7 kcal/mol.
source: Upon the addition of salt, N is destabilized by 0.7 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is a thermodynamic measurement from equilibrium unfolding experiments.

claim: I is destabilized less, by 0.4 kcal/mol with respect to the U state upon the addition of salt.
source: I is destabilized less, by 0.4 kcal/mol with respect to the U state (Table 3 and Figure 7)
evidence: This is a thermodynamic measurement documented in Table 3 and Figure 7.

claim: Force spectroscopy studies of the Syrian hamster prion protein (SHaPrP) had suggested that the U state sampled three off-pathway compact intermediates.
source: Force spectroscopy studies of the Syrian hamster prion protein (SHaPrP), had suggested that the U state sampled three off-pathway compact intermediates (Yu et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The occupancy of some of the off-pathway compact intermediates was more for a disease-linked mutant variant of the protein.
source: Force spectroscopy studies of the Syrian hamster prion protein (SHaPrP), had suggested that the U state sampled three off-pathway compact intermediates (Yu et al., 2012), and that the occupancy of some of these intermediates was more for a disease-linked mutant variant of the protein (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Disruption of the disulphide bond in the prion protein leads to its unfolding to a molten globule form.
source: More importantly, unlike the protein used in the current study, the protein used for the force spectroscopy measurements had a disrupted disulphide bond, and it is known that disruption of the disulphide bond in the prion protein leads to its unfolding to a molten globule form (Maiti and Surewicz, 2001; Honda, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several other studies have shown that SHaPrP (90-231) is natively structured at acidic pH.
source: In that study, the data appeared to suggest that the fluctuations might arise from the U state, but that could not have been the case because several other studies have shown that SHaPrP (90-231) is natively structured at acidic pH (Bjorndahl et al., 2011; Donne et al., 1997), including at pH 4 (Khan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The study of the native state dynamics of moPrP, across the α1-α3 and α2-α3 segments, monitored by the PET-FCS methodology, reveals three distinct processes, well-separated in time.
source: The study of the native state dynamics of moPrP, across the α1-α3 and α2-α3 segments, monitored by the PET-FCS methodology, using carefully designed single-free cysteine and single-tryptophan-containing variants, reveals three distinct processes, well-separated in time.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the PET-FCS experiments.

claim: The faster processes (~0.5–20 μs time constants) represent dynamics within the native state ensemble leading to the formation of the non-fluorescent complexes N* and N**.
source: The faster processes (~0.5–20 μs time constants) represent dynamics within the native state ensemble leading to the formation of the non-fluorescent complexes N* and N**.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PET-FCS data.

claim: The slow process (50–100 μs time constant) reports on the U ↔ I transition of folding.
source: The slow process (50–100 μs time constant) reports on the U ↔ I transition of folding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PET-FCS data in the context of folding.

claim: The rate constant of the N →N** transition, in the absence of salt, is an order of magnitude slower when measured by monitoring fluctuations across α2-α3, than for the fluctuations across α1-α3, possibly because the fluctuations across α2-α3 are slowed down by the disulphide bond, packing interactions and salt bridges in the core of the protein.
source: The rate constant of the N →N** transition, in the absence of salt, is an order of magnitude slower when measured by monitoring fluctuations across α2-α3, than for the fluctuations across α1-α3, possibly because the fluctuations across α2-α3 are slowed down by the disulphide bond, packing interactions and salt bridges in the core of the protein.
evidence: This is a comparison of rate constants with a speculative explanation.

claim: The folding landscape and the fluctuations within the native state ensemble are modulated by salt.
source: The folding landscape and the fluctuations within the native state ensemble are modulated by salt (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the salt-dependent experiments, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The addition of salt results in an increase in the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions, possibly because critical ionic interactions are lost.
source: The addition of salt results in an increase in the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions, possibly because critical ionic interactions are lost.
evidence: This is an observation with a speculative explanation.

claim: The enhancement of the time scale of native state fluctuations upon the addition of salt suggest that these fluctuations play a role in the initiation of misfolding of the protein.
source: The enhancement of the time scale of native state fluctuations upon the addition of salt, suggest that these fluctuations play a role in the initiation of misfolding of the protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the salt-dependent experiments.

claim: W144/C199-Atto moPrP is a mutant variant designed for PET-FCS measurements to monitor dynamics between helices α1 and α3.
source: In the case of W144/C199-Atto moPrP, W144 was used as the PET quencher of the Atto 655 moiety attached to the Cys residue at position 199, to report on the dynamics across helices α1 and α3 (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the design of one of the experimental constructs, shown in Figure 1.

claim: W171/C225-Atto moPrP is a mutant variant designed for PET-FCS measurements to monitor dynamics between helices α2 and α3.
